newsitem.title: GERMANY: FOCUS-Bonn rules out new tax "summit"-sources.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Bonn rules out new tax "summit"-sources.

text.p: The prospect of a new "tax summit" with opposition Social Democrats (SPD) receded on Wednesday when government sources ruled out a repeat of their bid earlier this year to get cross-party support for a major tax reform.

Bonn is relying on the reform, which aims to cut 30 billion marks ($17.6 billion) of taxes over the next two years, to kickstart growth in the sluggish German economy just before and after the planned start of European monetary union in 1999.

Speaking after a meeting of senior coalition politicians in Bonn, the sources said the government had now decided future contact with the SPD on the reform would take place within work groups that form part of the standard parliamentary process.
With the SPD controlling the upper house of the German parliament, the decision to forego special talks risks delaying the tax-cutting reforms which the government wants to introduce from next year.
It also runs against reports that beleagered Finance Minister Theo Waigel, quoted earlier on Wednesday in the mass circulation Bild newspaper, had renewed an offer for further talks with the SPD.

The sources criticised the SPD's newly-launched alternative scheme to restructure some 78 billion marks of tax revenues in a budget-neutral way as containing little content worth holding special talks to discuss.
The comments crushed hopes for a deal that grew earlier in the day after a top SPD official said he could agree in principle to a significant cut in the top level of income tax.

The Cologne-based Express newspaper quoted SPD parliamentary business manager Peter Struck in an interview as saying he could accept a cut in the top tax rate from the current 53 percent to 45 percent, a move in the direction of the 39 percent that Bonn wants.
Until now the Social Democrats have criticised such a move as a "gift to the rich" and said it would in any case be difficult to finance given the stretched state of German finances.
In April, they walked out of special talks with the government aimed at getting cross-party support for a new tax bill.

Rainer Bruederle, deputy chairman of the Free Democrats (FDP), Chancellor Helmut Kohl's junior coalition partners and the most vocal supporters of tax cuts, said Struck's comments showed that the will existed among the SPD for agreement.

"It shows...that the SPD has finally moved a bit and that it must be possible...to come to an agreement," Bruederle said on German radio. He had earlier been quoted in a newspaper as saying he would be happy with a rate of 41 percent. ($ = 1.702 German Marks)
